title: FLORA CITY COUNCIL MEEETS
full_story:
The Flora City Council met Monday afternoon and heard three requests from local residents about differing topics.

The first to speak to commissioners was April Carruthers from the Clay County Health Department to request the use of the REA Building at the Clay County Fairgrounds.  She says they are looking to host their 4th Annual Trick or Treat Street on October 8, from 3:30-8:00pm.  They are also hosting Explore-a- Truck that evening. Local agencies and vehicles seeking to participate are encouraged to apply by calling April at 618-662-4406 to sign up.  The council approved her request unanimously.

Next, Cat Osterholz with Clip and Tip Strays (C.A.T.S) appeared before commissioners again to once again explain the non-profit group’s mission of reducing the stray and feral cat population in Clay County and particularly Flora by utilizing TNR (Trap Neuter Return).  She says there are at least 14 feral cat colonies in the city and they have sterilized 98 cats in town and a total of 226 within the county in an effort to reduce the number of cats being born in the colonies.  Cats can begin reproducing at four months old and she gave evidence of that very thing happening.  She says kittens are born and people take them to shelters only to be turned away because they are full.  Osterholz added TNR is a long term solution to the overpopulation problem, but it takes some time for the full benefit to become apparent.  But there is a noticeable difference being made.  She further explained their mission and the work being done, but it is not free.  Reduced cost…yes, but still not free.  She asked the city if they could help by participating to the program.  She asked for $10,000 for the full year, but said they would accept any help they could get.  Mayor Spicer thanked the group for their work and said the council would take her request under advisement.

The final visitor was the second straight appearance by resident Anthony Krutsinger.  He appeared at the last meeting to object to the expanding use of Flock Safety equipment around the country and specifically in Flora.  The cameras are capable of reading license plates on passing vehicles on certain streets in towns where they are deployed, including Flora.  Krutsinger asked Flora Police Chief Jeremy Ruger if the cameras recorded audio, to which he replied no they do not.  He continued by asking if the cameras are multi-directional, with Chief Ruger saying no they are not.  He asked who is trained to use them and was told the Chief and a limited number of people.  Krutsinger asked about oversight and didn’t wait for the answer of the leadership as he moved on to criticize the opinion that they are an invasion of privacy and he hopes they are outlawed.  Chief Ruger stated that would be up to the state government and legislative leaders.  Krutsinger continued with statements that there is evidence that there is corruption in the use of the cameras by those charged with their administration, but did not offer specific evidence and closed by stating that many are unhappy with their use and some communities are removing them at the request of their citizens.  He asked Flora leaders to reconsider their use and seek public input before their use is continued and/or expanded.

Mayor Spicer then asked commissioners to approve the meeting agenda and consent agenda, which they quickly did.  The latter included past meeting minutes, the warrant list, treasurer’s report police activity report and building and zoning report.

In regular business, the mayor sought to appoint John Casolari to the Police Pension Fund for a period of two-years that expires 6/15/28.  Her request was approved by the council unanimously,

Commissioner Jeremy Henderson sought the approval of a lease agreement between the City of Flora and Clint Green doing business as Little Toot Railroad.  The ordinance was approved without dissent.  Henderson added that Green is expecting the state to complete their inspection of the railroad in the days ahead and he intends to be open June 27/28.  He also stated that Green is seeking to purchase of another engine.

Commissioner Phil Wiley took a moment to invite everyone to the expanding Community Market on Saturday mornings from 8:00-Noon at Flora’s Library Park.  He said fresh produce is now being offered more frequently as the growing season is fully underway.  He says to come hungry because there is good food available from participating vendors and there are gifts to be found and something for everybody including tips for care for your garden and plants at home.  Wiley also took a moment to thank everyone who attended the Spirit of 1776 event on Sunday.  He said there was an unbelievable turnout as people celebrated America’s 250th birthday.  Wiley added that it was a beautiful day and the community and several churches participated in the festivities.  He closed by thanking organizers, ESDA, volunteer firemen and city employees who were put into service before and after it concluded.

Commissioner Lacey Lewis said that Flora Tourism is still in need of volunteers to help with Flora’s July 4th celebration.  They are still looking for people to help with the water inflatables and for people to man the admission gates at Charley Brown Park to accept payment as people pour in for the celebration.  Lewis said people who would like to help should contact Arriel Dulaney at the Flora Chamber of Commerce in Flora’s Historic B & O Railroad Depot.

Flora City Administrator/Economic Development Director Mike Stanford presented two action items.  First, Stanford presented an ordinance for the funding agreement with the State of Illinois for the sidewalk project on N. Worthey from W. 8th St to Walmart in the amount of $85,700, with the state providing $77,130 and Flora contributing $8,570 to the project.  The motion passed unanimously.  Stanford then sought approval for a Intermediary Relending Program Loan in the amount of $62,500 for Jaydon and Jeffrey Yates for their new business Flora Garden Center and Landscaping on State St.  That motion also passed unanimously.

Building and Zoning Official Chad Bayles presented two items for consideration.  The first was an ordinance approving a variance to Devin and Destiny Dannells for the placement of a pool in their front yard on a corner lot on Rider St.  The variance was approved without dissent, as was the second ordinance granting a variance on the construction of a privacy fence in their front yard on Rider St.  Bayles also called attention to a phone call he received from a church in Crawfordsville, IN.  He said the church has a program called Destination Unknown, where they go to other communities to seek volunteer work, they can do.  He said they asked to come to Flora to work and when they came, they painted the gate and bridge at the entrance to Charley Brown Park and did a good job.  Mayor Spicer sought to thank and recognize the group for their effort.

The final item on the agenda was from Superintendent of Public Services Toby Rinehart.  He presented an Intergovernmental Agreement with the Village of Iuka for Mosquito Spraying, which was quickly approved.  With all business complete, the meeting adjourned.

title: FLORA SCHOOL BOARD
full_story:
The Flora School Board met in regular session last night.  The Board voted to renew the District Insurance, renew membership for IASB, approved an intergovernmental agreement between Flora Library and the school district and approved the amended budget for the 2025-2026 school year.

The Board recognized the state qualifiers for junior high track, high school track, high school boys’ tennis, and Bass Club.  They also recognized the high school softball team on winning Regionals and making it to Sectionals.   The board approved the FHJHS officials pay for the next school year and a CD investment bid submitted by Flora Bank and Trust.

Superintendent Dr. Joel Hackney highlighted the end of the year lunch and recognition of staff as well as providing an update on the summer maintenance and cleaning and the progress towards district goals and objectives.

In personnel matters the board accepted the resignation as junior high softball coach submitted by Jordyn Strange and recalled Holly Britton as paraprofessional and Bristol Burroughs as Pre-K Parent Coordinator Paraprofessional for the next school year.  They also approved Cathy Taylor and Matea Petrea as freshman class sponsors, Reghan Warren as junior class sponsor, Matea Petrea as a volunteer assistant volleyball coach, Ruthie Griffith as 8th grade girls’ basketball coach, and Steve Valbert, Benny Allen, Matt Lindeman, Dylan Shroyer, Mark Long, Timmy Sharp, and Rick Gibbs as volunteer bass club sponsors contingent on background screening.

title: OLNEY SUSPECT DIES
full_story:
Illinois State Police (ISP) Division of Criminal Investigation Zone 8 is assisting the Richland County Sheriff’s Office with a death investigation in Olney.

About 3:30 am on Monday, June 8th the Richland County Sheriff’s Office responded to a domestic disturbance at a residence in the 4500 block of East Golf Lane in Olney.  A deputy located the suspect, 49-year-old Kenneth Lee Grove, who failed to comply with the deputy’s commands, at which time the deputy deploy his Taser.  Grove became unresponsive, and emergency medical services were requested.  The deputy began life‑saving measures; however, Grove was pronounced deceased on scene.

The Richland County Sheriff’s Office requested ISP investigate the incident.

title: FLORA POLICE ACTIVITY REPORT
full_story:
Flora Chief of Jeremy Ruger released his Activity Report for May during Monday’s Flora City Council meeting.

During the month, Flora police officers investigated 9 traffic accidents.

They made six criminal arrests.  There was one drug arrest and no DUI arrests during May.  There were two local ordinance arrests, 10 traffic arrests and 5 warrant arrests.

Officers issued 28 warning tickets, responded to 20 alarms and had 1,083 calls for service and had one juvenile contact.

Also, Flora police officers drove 4,503 miles and conducted 52 investigations during May.  They answered 269, 911 calls and conducted 14 UTV Inspections and no Golf Cart Inspections during May.

title: IGNITE CURIOSITY SUMMER CAMPS
full_story:
Olney Central College is inviting area students of all ages to explore new interests and develop hands-on skills through its upcoming Ignite Curiosity Summer Camps.  Registration is now underway for the camps which offer creativity and teamwork for a variety of age groups.

Getting Styled meets from 9:30 to 2:30 on June 17th at the Terry L. Bruce West Richland Center in Noble and is for grades 8-12, the cost is at $25 per camper.  STEM Builders, 3D Printing Camp meets from 8:00 to 12 noon on July 20th in the OCC Learning Commons Stem Lab and is for grades 8-12, the cost is also $25 per camper.

To learn more about these camps at OCC or about other camps at the other IECC campuses in Fairfield, Mt. Carmel, or Robinson, go to the iecc.edu/communityed website.  To sign up or register for the OCC camps, call or visit the Student Services Office at Olney Central College.

title: FLORA BUILDING AND ZONING REPORT
full_story:
Flora Building and Zoning Official Chad Bayles presented the monthly building and zoning report for May during Monday’s Flora City Council meeting.

The report shows two new residential construction projects were undertaken in May, valued at $102,237.

And there were no new industrial projects started during May.

There were two total new projects in Flora for May, valued at $102,237 with $175 collected in permit fees and $50 in deposit fees for May

The year-to-date figures show 31 total residential projects so far this year with a value of $531,020.

There are four year-to-date commercial projects valued at $17,444,334 and no new industrial projects.

That makes 35 total projects valued at $17,975,354, with $2,108 in permit fees and $600 in deposit fees collected for the year.

title: 2 ELECTED TO WAYNE-WHITE BOARD
full_story:
Blaine Norton and Ryan Duckworth were elected as new members of the Wayne-White Counties Electric Cooperative Board of Directors.  The two won their contested races during a vote at the cooperative’s annual meeting Friday night in Wayne City.

To represent District 2, Blaine Norton of Fairfield defeated board member Vernon Gwaltney.  A Wayne-White member since 2003, Norton works in nuclear medicine, holding a Master’s Degree in Imaging Science, Nuclear Medicine Advanced Association from the University of Arkansas School for Medical Sciences.

To represent District 3, Ryan Duckworth defeated Nick McKinney.  Born and raised in White County, Duckworth moved south of Fairfield in southern Wayne County in 2012.  A local farmer and part-owner of Duckworth and Smith Farms, Inc., he has been a co-op member since 1997.

In District 6, David Hunsinger of Carmi ran unopposed for a first full term on the board.  Hunsinger was appointed to the board in February, 2024 to fill an unexpired term.  He is a grain farmer and manager of Oilwell Service at Eastern Services.

title: PHARMACY GRANTS
full_story:
Governor JB Pritzker announced Friday that 434 Illinois pharmacies will receive nearly $25 million in support, the first distribution of annual funding established through legislation he signed last year.  The Sav Mor Pharmacy in Louisville is among those receiving funding.

The fund was designed to assist pharmacies most at risk of closure or financial strain, especially those in rural and low-income communities with limited healthcare access.  The pot was split equally between all eligible applicants, with each pharmacy receiving $56,892.

The money was established under bipartisan legislation Pritzker signed last July.  The bill, known as the Prescription Drug Affordability Act, put new regulations on pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, companies that are responsible for negotiating drug prices between employer health insurance plans and pharmaceutical drug companies.

They have been the target of intense scrutiny in recent years, facing accusations of steering patients toward their own affiliated pharmacies and designing healthcare pricing formulas that boost their own profits rather than patient savings, including a lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission against the three largest PBMS for their alleged use of anticompetitive practices to artificially inflate insulin prices.

The first $25 million in fees collected were placed in a special fund for independent pharmacies, which can use the money to support existing operations, as well as expansions of business hours and new offerings, such as telepharmacy services, remote consultations and medication delivery.

The program, administered by the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity and the Illinois Retail Merchants Association, granted funding to pharmacies in 252 cities scattered across 94 of the state’s 102 counties.  Prioritized were pharmacies in rural or medically underserved communities and small independent pharmacies with fewer than 10 locations.
